posts.style: Design & Aspiration · The View, Then the Seat
posts.alt: Cardiff-by-the-Sea coastal backyard at sunset with a rectangular vanishing-edge pool and a raised spa spilling a sheet of water into it, silver travertine deck and coping, modern chaise loungers with concrete side tables, olive trees, agave and feather grass, and the Pacific horizon beyond
posts.hook: A coastal lot gives you the view for free. The design decides whether you ever sit in it.
posts.caption:
Everyone with a lot like this leads with the ocean. The harder question is where you actually sit to watch it.

So the whole yard is built around one sightline. The pool runs a vanishing edge that drops the far coping out of view, so the water reads as if it spills straight into the sea. The spa sits raised just behind it, spilling its own sheet back into the pool — the sound arrives before you do. The deck is silver travertine because it stays cool underfoot on a west-facing lot at 5pm, and the planting stays low — agave, feather grass, olives — so nothing ever competes with the horizon.

Get the view for free. Then spend the budget on the one seat you'll use every evening.

The selections:
• vanishing-edge pool
• raised spa with spillway
• glass-tile spa face
• silver travertine deck & coping
• olive trees, agave & feather grass

posts.alt: El Cajon single-story home at dusk with a wide large-format stamped-concrete driveway in a random-slate pattern, a charcoal brick soldier-course border band, a raised stucco planter with agave and succulents, warm path lighting and a glowing front entry
posts.hook: The driveway is the biggest thing on the front of your house. Most people spend the least on it.
posts.caption:
It's the first surface every guest stands on and the last thing the street sees — and it's usually a plain gray slab that cracked in year three.

This one does the opposite work. The field is large-format stamped concrete in a random-slate pattern, so a big run of driveway reads as stone instead of a parking pad. The charcoal soldier-course border draws a clean line around the whole thing — that single band is what makes it look designed rather than poured. The raised planter breaks up the mass with agave and succulents, and the low path lights turn the approach into an entrance after dark instead of a black strip.

Same footprint every house on the block has. It just stops looking like a driveway and starts looking like the front of a home someone thought about.

The selections:
• large-format stamped concrete, random-slate pattern
• charcoal soldier-course border band
• raised stucco planter
• agave & succulent planting
• low-voltage path & entry lighting

Want the front of the house to finally match the back? DM “DESIGN”.

posts.style: Craft & Process · The Wall Is the Work
posts.alt: Tierrasanta canyon-rim backyard at dusk with a circular sunken fire lounge built from board-formed concrete curved seat walls around a linear concrete gas fire trough burning over lava rock, gray concrete-paver patio and path, agave and aloe planting, and dark hills behind
posts.hook: Anyone can set a fire in the ground. The hard part is the curved wall around it.
posts.caption:
The flame gets the photo. The concrete is the actual build.

Those curved seat walls are board-formed — poured against real timber boards so the grain of the wood prints into the concrete face. You only get that texture, and a true circle that holds its line, if the formwork is built right the first time; there's no fixing a board-formed wall after the pour. It's the slow, invisible half of the job. The fire itself is a linear trough burning over lava rock, set low so it warms the seat without blocking the sightline across the canyon, with a step light tucked into the wall so nobody misses the grade change in the dark.

The part that took the most skill is the part that just looks like a wall. That's usually how it goes.

The selections:
• board-formed concrete seat walls
• linear gas fire trough with lava rock
• concrete-paver patio & path
• integrated low-voltage step lighting
• agave & aloe planting

Want the seat built as well as the fire? DM “DESIGN”.

posts.style: Lifestyle · Where the Night Actually Lands
posts.alt: Scripps Ranch backyard after dark under a black louvered aluminum pergola strung with cafe lights, a built-in Bull grill in a stucco island with stainless doors and drawers, a raised concrete bar top with upholstered barstools and a sink, stamped-concrete pavers, olive trees and a Spanish tile-roof home behind
posts.hook: Nobody stands around the couch. They stand around whoever's cooking.
posts.caption:
Every party ends up in the same ten feet — wherever the food and the drinks are. This yard just built that spot on purpose, outside.

The louvered aluminum pergola is the quiet hero: the blades tilt to throw shade at 4pm and open up for the string lights at 8, so the same square works in July heat and October dark. Under it, a Bull grill and stainless cabinetry give you a real kitchen, not a cart, and the raised bar top turns the cook into part of the conversation instead of facing a wall. Stamped-concrete pavers underfoot take the foot traffic and the spilled drinks and still look like stone.

Stop hosting from the kitchen window. Build the ten feet everyone was going to crowd into anyway.

The selections:
• louvered aluminum pergola
• Bull built-in grill & stainless cabinetry
• raised concrete bar top with barstools
• cafe string lighting
• stamped-concrete pavers

posts.style: Trust & Difference · One Contract, One Firm
posts.alt: 4S Ranch courtyard at dusk with a sunken travertine fire-pit lounge ringed by curved seat walls with cushions, a covered outdoor kitchen with a Bull grill and beverage fridge and stone counters, a separate lounge seating area, cafe string lights overhead, an olive tree, agave and a two-story Spanish tile-roof home
posts.hook: Count the trades in this one photo. Now imagine hiring each of them yourself.
posts.caption:
One frame: a sunken fire lounge, a covered kitchen, the paving that ties them together, the gas lines under both, the low-voltage lighting over all of it, the masonry, the framing on that roof. That's five or six trades meeting in the same courtyard.

Hire them separately and you become the general contractor by accident — the one deciding whose base the travertine sits on, why the kitchen gas wasn't roughed in before the pavers went down, who owns the crack that shows up at the hearth. These projects rarely fail inside a trade. They fail in the seams between them.

We carry the whole thing on one contract, under one Class B license (CSLB #1139785) — our own crew and our long-trusted subcontractors, scheduled and answerable to one firm. One plan, one number, one company accountable for the seams. You just get to live in it.

The selections:
• travertine paving & fire-pit lounge
• curved concrete seat walls
• covered outdoor kitchen with Bull grill & beverage fridge
• cafe string lighting
• olive trees & agave

Want one firm accountable for the whole yard? DM “DESIGN”.
